newsitem.title: USA: Ill. incinerator bond case ruling set for Sept. 30.
newsitem.headline: Ill. incinerator bond case ruling set for Sept. 30.

text.p: A Cook County, Ill., Circuit Court judge will rule by Sept. 30 on whether to dismiss a lawsuit brought against state of Illinois officials by incinerator developers and bondholders.
Following two and a half hours of oral arguments Monday afternoon on the state's motions to dismiss all the counts in the case, Judge Edwin Berman said he would issue a ruling on or before Sept. 30.

Lawyers representing Illinois Commerce Commission officials, who were sued in March by the developers of two-bond financed waste-tire incinerators, argued that an amendment to Illinois' Retail Rate Act did not impair any contract involving the incinerators.

The lawsuit, which was filed by incinerator developer CGE Ford Heights and joined by CGE Fulton, the developer of another incinerator, and by bondholders, claimed that the state's repeal of an incinerator subsidy was unconstitutional in that it impaired contracts and violated equal protection provisions.
The lawsuit also claimed the amendment to the Retail Rate Act was improperly passed and that it constituted special legislation.

The Illinois General Assembly amended the Retail Rate Act in January, removing a state subsidy that guarenteed incinerators a higher rate at which they could sell electricity they produced to utilities. Gov. Jim Edgar signed the measure into law on March 14.

By that time, nearly $500 million of tax-exempt bonds had been sold to finance three incinerators in Illinois, including $79.5 million of bonds sold for the Ford Heights project in 1994 and $84.6 million of bonds sold for an incinerator in Fulton last December.

Lawyers Steven Varick and Rick Redmond of McBride Baker & Coles argued that that the only contract that existed was between the developers and Commonwealth Edison Co. for the purchase of electricity, which they said was not impaired by the amendment because the contract also provided for a lower wholesale rate for electricity sales. In addition, they said the Retail Rate Act itself did not contain language intended to create contractual rights, as does some other laws.
The lawyers also contended that bondholders rights were not impaired by the new law because their security interest in the CGE Ford Heights project remained the same.
"Bondholders here are relying on the continuation of a general statute...if you could, the state legislature would be precluded from making any changes in public policy," Redmond said.
Varick said bondholders, which he listed as high-yield mutual funds, made a bet that Illinois' rate subsidy would remain.
"They lost and would like this court to intervene on their behalf," he said.

Jeff Hall, an attorney at Bartlit Beck Herman Palenchar & Scott, who is representing the incinerator developers, said there was an implied contract with the state that induced the developers to act on the incentive the state was offering since 1987 to incinerators.

Hall said that the Illinois Commerce Commission signed off on the projects, and in the case of Ford Heights that facility was built and was currently in federal bankruptcy court as a result of the lost subsidy.
"We have not only an impairment, but a destruction of our contracts," he said.

William Schaller, an attorney at Baker & McKenzie, who is representing bondholders, contended the bonds issued for the Ford Heights project were state of Illinois bonds because they were issued through the Illinois Development Finance Authority.
"In this case, the state was an integral player in this market," he said.
Varick countered that the authority was just a conduit issuer for the project that ensured tax-exempt status for the bonds.
A second lawsuit brought by the Illinois subsidiaries of Forter Wheeler Corp., the developer of a $320 million bond-financed incinerator in Robbins, is pending in U.S. District Court in Chicago.
--Karen Pierog, 312-408-8647
